name: Rangkas
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.source_named: Rangkas (extinct West Himalayish): sketch in Grierson 1909, Linguistic Survey of India Vol. III Pt. 1; Widmer 2014/2022 discuss it; no online copy opened.

sources.citation: Nishi, Yoshio. 1991. ヒマラヤ諸語の分布と分類（中）. 国立民族学博物館研究報告 16(1): 31-158.
sources.note: Bibliographic note only: D.D. Sharma 1989 Part One 'contains a description of the phonology and grammar of Johari (= Rangkas)'.

sources.citation: Sharma, D.D. 1989. Tribal Languages of Himachal Pradesh, Part I (Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages II). Delhi: Mittal Publications.
sources.note: Not a Rangkas description. p.2: 'Rangkas, the dialect of Johar is lost to us for ever, due to the shift of Johari speakers to the Kumauni dialect of the region.' Shows that each sketch in this series carries a 'Supra-segmental phonemes / Accent' subsection (Pattani 2.8.3, Tinani 1.2.2b, Gahri 2.6), so the companion 'Johari' chapter probably has one too.

sources.citation: Saxena, Anju & Lars Borin (eds). 2022. Synchronic and Diachronic Aspects of Kanashi. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton (open access).
sources.note: Table 11 p.185 names 'Rangkas (D. D. Sharma 1989b: 195-254)' as its Rangkas source, confirming that Sharma's 'Johari' chapter is the modern Rangkas sketch; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Saxena, Anju. 2022. The Linguistic Landscape of the Indian Himalayas (Brill's Studies in South and Southwest Asian Languages 14). Leiden: Brill (open access).
sources.note: Single footnote mention of Johari (clusivity, after D.D. Sharma 1989); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Willis, Christina M. 2007. A Descriptive Grammar of Darma: An Endangered Tibeto-Burman Language. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin.
sources.note: p.21: Rangkas 'is classified as extinct (Driem 2001: 934; S.R. Sharma 2001b; Gordon 2005)'; classification discussion only, nothing on Rangkas phonology.

sources.citation: Sharma, Suhnu Ram. 2001. A Study on the Tibeto-Burman Languages of Uttar Pradesh. In Nagano & LaPolla (eds), New Research on Zhangzhung and Related Himalayan Languages (Senri Ethnological Reports 19), 187-194. Osaka: National Museum of Ethnology.
sources.note: Sec. 2.7 'Rangkas or Saukiya Khun': no speakers found by Srivastava (1953 survey) or on the author's own field trip; 'In all possibility it has died out already.' Nothing on phonology.

sources.citation: Sharma, D.D. 1989. [Pronominalization in Tibeto-Himalayan languages]. Panjab University Research Bulletin (Arts) XX(1). Chandigarh: Panjab University.
sources.note: Cites Johari verb forms (taken from the LSI specimens) for pronominalization only; nothing on accent.

sources.citation: Grierson, G.A. (ed.; section by Sten Konow). 1909. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. III: Tibeto-Burman Family, Part I. Calcutta: Superintendent of Government Printing. 'Rangkas or Saukiya Khun', pp. 479ff.
sources.note: p.480, 'Pronunciation': "We have no information regarding accentuation or tones." Data are written specimens forwarded by Babu Gobind Prasad; phonetic system said to be 'broadly the same as in the neighbouring dialects of Almora'. Explicitly silent.

sources.citation: Bhatt, Uma & Shekhar Pathak (eds). 2015. The Languages of Uttarakhand (People's Linguistic Survey of India vol. 30). New Delhi: Orient Blackswan. 'Johari' chapter.

sources.note: Glottolog codes its Johari chapter to Rangkas [rgk]; if it treats the TB language rather than the present Kumaoni-based speech of the Johari Shauka, it may carry a phonology note.

sources.citation: Sharma, D.D. 1989. Johari. In: Tibeto-Himalayan Languages of Uttarakhand, Part One (Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages III), pp. 195-254. New Delhi: Mittal Publications. ISBN 81-7099-171-4.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.access_detail: print only, per the reader; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: The only modern phonology+grammar sketch of Rangkas (= 'Johari'); Glottolog's sole descriptive ref, used as the Rangkas source by Saxena & Borin 2022. Sharma's parallel sketches in the same series all carry a 'Supra-segmental phonemes / Accent' subsection, so if any accent statement for Rangkas exists in print it is here (though probably inferred from LSI written specimens, since Sharma himself calls the dialect lost).

sources.citation: van Driem, George. 2001. Languages of the Himalayas, vol. 2, p. 934 (Rangkas). Leiden: Brill.
